extracted.intended_audience: researchers, research administrators, and policy-makers interested in NIH funding and peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing how well NIH peer-review scores predict grant 'success' and whether the current peer-review funding process is cost-effective and robust. The page reports research findings and policy suggestions about NIH grant allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive power of NIH peer-review percentile scores
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH Peer Review Percentile Scores are Poorly Predictive of Grant Productivity — the mechanism used to allocate funds based on top scores works essentially no better than distributing those dollars at random.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reanalysis showed very little difference between top-ranked projects and those ranked in the 20th percentile when measuring future citation impact; while average productivity for better scores was somewhat higher, differences were extremely small, raising questions about whether the effort of ranking is worthwhile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success metric: papers produced and citation counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the success of a research grant by determining how many papers resulted from the work and how many times those papers are cited in future research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cited study (and the original dataset) used number of resulting publications and subsequent citation counts as the operational definition of grant productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding percentile thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH historically funds proposals around top percentiles (recently around the top 10%); the study focused analysis on the top 20% of grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because funding is limited, selection cutoffs matter; the study found small differences within the top 20%, and noted NIH often only funds near the top 10% in recent years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrimination capability of peer review (good vs bad science)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review can discriminate between very good science and very bad science — i.e., between grants in the top 20% and those below the 50th percentile — but is poor at fine-grained ranking among the top proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis found meaningful separation when comparing top-tier to low-tier grants, but limited ability to predict which top-tier grants will produce the most-cited work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-effectiveness of peer review (financial costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review imposes substantial financial costs (e.g., NIH Center for Scientific Review budget about $110 million annually, plus institute spending) that could instead fund additional grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given limited budget and small predictive gains from fine-grained ranking, the researchers argue the money spent on peer review might be better allocated directly to research funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity cost: time and diversion from research
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing and reviewing grant proposals is extremely time-consuming and diverts scientists from doing science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond direct financial costs, the labor burden on applicants and reviewers represents an important consideration in evaluating the value of detailed peer-review ranking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjectivity and susceptibility to single negative opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: The peer review process allows substantial subjectivity; the objection of a single committee member can effectively kill a grant proposal regardless of whether that objection is legitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High sensitivity to individual opinions can undermine the fairness and robustness of selection, and may make the process worse than random allocation when opinions dominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative selection mechanism: lottery for top proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed solution is to use peer review to identify a pool of top proposals and then award grants at random (a lottery) among that pool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note historical and contemporary uses of lotteries (e.g., military draft, magnet school admissions, residency applications, some New Zealand scientific grants) as precedents; this could reduce ranking costs while preserving basic quality control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questioning the value of fine-grained ranking effort
rubrics_metrics.description: The differences in productivity between better-scored grants and slightly lower-scored grants are extremely small, suggesting the effort spent on fine-grained ranking might not be justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers suggest resources and effort currently devoted to ranking applications could be redirected, given small marginal returns from distinguishing among the top proposals.
